cards.title: Write story-based emails using the vivid-in-the-moment structure
cards.summary: Turn generic 'I worked hard' backstories into sensory, incident-driven stories that pull readers into your offer email.
cards.use_when: Writing the story email in a welcome, nurture, or promotion sequence, or any email meant to build engagement and emotional investment before the offer.
steps: Recognize that most people write summarized stories: 'I was working long hours, low pay, no chance of promotion, so I started my online business.' This is flat and skimmable.

Rewrite the same story as a lived moment: 'One day I worked hard labor until my back was throbbing. I was only 20 but felt the aches of a 59-year-old with arthritis. All for my boss to tell us at the end of the day we'd get behind schedule if we didn't work harder. That's when I knew I couldn't take it anymore and decided to start my business today.'
Convert abstract conditions (low pay, no promotion) into one specific incident with physical detail, a person, and a line of dialogue.
Place the story so it leads directly into the offer or lesson — the emotion from the incident carries the reader into the CTA.
Apply the same technique to the reader's world: the incident that triggered their search for your product.
caveats: Source asserts this style 'gets clients very good results'; that is a practitioner claim, not a measured benchmark.
Borrowed-authority framing (citing a nine-figure business's emails) is the source's method, not required.

cards.title: Value density over total length in any piece of copy
cards.summary: Judging copy by value-per-minute (or per-sentence) rather than raw length is what separates high-performing assets from bloated ones.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a landing page, sales email, ad script, or product description for length and fluff before publishing.
steps: Apply the source's principle from its own viral video: it recorded 7 hours of content and published only the best 4, and that density is cited as the reason it performed.
For each paragraph or section, ask: if I removed this, would the reader lose information needed to buy? If no, cut it.
Do not add length to look thorough. 'I'm not belaboring any points... everything in here is densely packed with value.'
For store copy, the same test applies to PDP descriptions, shipping/returns explanations, and email paragraphs — a tighter asset is more likely to hold attention and be acted on.
Treat long-form as a container for high-density content, not an excuse for repetition.
caveats: The viral-video view counts cited are the source's own examples, not a guaranteed outcome for your assets.
Density does not replace the need for sufficient information — cutting needed detail hurts conversion.

cards.title: Use the incident-motivation-complacency (IMC) cycle to time email outreach
cards.summary: People only buy when an incident creates motivation, so the job of a long email list is to be present at every cycle, not to convert on the first squeeze.
cards.use_when: Planning an email send cadence and deciding how often to re-approach dormant subscribers or lapsed customers.
steps: Map the cycle: Incident → Motivation → Action → Complacency → (new Incident).

Incident: the specific event that breaks a person's inertia — stepping on a scale after 6 months, a shirt fitting too tight, a friend's passing comment. Recognition of the problem is often sudden and specific.
Motivation: the emotional state created by the incident, which drives the Action (signing up, buying).
Complacency: after acting, resistance (hunger on a diet, a busy week, a missed email) sets in and they forget or abandon.

Implication for sends: keep sending. Because you cannot know whose incident just happened, frequency plus good copy is how you catch the person at the right point in their cycle. For an online store, this supports sustained campaigns to past buyers and list subscribers rather than one-shot blasts.
Read list inactivity as complacency, not rejection — a new selling event can re-enter them into motivation.
caveats: This is a practitioner framework from a service/outreach context; the source gives no measured conversion lift.
Do not confuse 'keep sending' with sending irrelevant emails — copy still has to offer value or a real reason to buy.

cards.title: Follow up with different angles on a fixed rhythm
cards.summary: A specific follow-up cadence — bump, wait, second angle, wait, third angle, then move on — is the structure the source credits with converting stalled prospects.
cards.use_when: Following up on abandoned carts, cold leads, unanswered partnership or wholesale emails, or any sequence where the first message got no reply.
steps: Send the opening message, then wait about 3 days.

Send a short bump: 'Just wondering if you saw this' or 'bumping this up in case it got buried.' This is the only time to use that exact bump. To vary it for ecommerce, keep the same brevity but change the reference point (e.g., 'checking in on the restock question').
Wait another 2–3 days with no reply, then send a second, different-angle message — if the first was light and funny, go serious; if the first offered one thing, offer something else.
Wait another 2–3 days, then a third angle. If there is still zero reply, move on.
Key asymmetry: it is far easier to move someone from maybe to yes than from no to maybe. Prioritize warm leads and don't burn your effort chasing fully cold ones.
If someone said no outright, leave them alone for at least a month before circling back.
caveats: The 2–3 day intervals and the one-month cool-off are the source's heuristics, not tested benchmarks for every business.
Warm leads who say yes then go cold should keep getting followed up 'until they eventually hire you' — adapt this to marketing compliance (unsubscribe, consent) in your region.

cards.title: Borrow media-buying logic: stay top of mind for the moment of incident
cards.summary: Big brands keep advertising to people who already know them because they are waiting for the incident that makes someone act, and being first to mind is the win.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep spending on brand retention campaigns, retargeting, or reminder ads for a known audience.
steps: Accept the premise: you are not trying to teach awareness to people who already know you; you are trying to be the name they think of when their problem suddenly becomes urgent.
The McDonald's example works because the incident (hungry, driving past) meets the placement (the arches nearby). The ad budget exists to occupy that moment, not to introduce the brand.
Ecommerce translation: keep your products in front of past buyers and list subscribers through reminder emails, retargeting, and seasonal sends, so when the need arises, you are the default.
Judge these campaigns on whether they get the impression and the mind-share, not only on the last-click conversion in the same session.
Build the 'incident' language into copy — name the trigger event (running out, a season change, an upcoming event) so the reader recognizes their moment.
caveats: This is reasoning by analogy from mass-market fast food; it does not prove that the same ad spend pays back for a small store.
Source provides no attribution or incrementality method — pair with your own measurement if budget is tight.

cards.title: Send a three-email sample pack showing range (promo, story, value)
cards.summary: A ready sample sequence — one promo email, one story email, one value email — is a compact way to demonstrate email skill and get a reply.
cards.use_when: Approaching a store with an underused email list, a wholesale partner with a newsletter, or a brand you want to write for — or as a model for your own welcome sequence.
steps: State plainly at the top what the pack is — e.g., 'This sample pack contains three emails showcasing how I write to nurture and convert leads.'
Include exactly three emails, each a different type: (1) a promotion email, (2) a story email, (3) a value/teaching email.
Make all three about the specific prospect's product or niche so they can imagine them on their own list.
Deliver with a soft line: 'I noticed you send emails — wanted to pass these over to see if anything is usable on your list.' Do not hard-pitch before they respond.
Use the same three-email architecture when building your own welcome flow: one email that tells the origin story, one that teaches something useful, one that makes the offer.
caveats: The source's success examples ('these emails are great', leading to the client) are anecdotes, not guarantees.
If the prospect has no list, switch to a different sample asset (PDP rewrite, ad creative) instead.

cards.title: Build a sales-page skeleton in a doc to preview structure before writing
cards.summary: A placeholder sales page — headline, scroll-stopper, text, scroll-stopper, text — communicates structure and effort before the real copy exists.
cards.use_when: Pitching a landing page or PDP rewrite internally or to a partner, or outlining a long-form offer page before writing full copy.
steps: Create the skeleton in a document, using the same section order as a real sales page.
Start with the headline at the top — the source treats it as the single most important element and the thing the eye should hit first.
Alternate 'scroll-stopper' visual breaks with text blocks, repeating the pattern down the page. This mirrors how a real page consumes attention in chunks.
Use literal placeholders if needed — the source says its template words were made up on the spot. The goal is that the reader can conceptualize the finished page.
Format the doc so it reads visually like a real page on scroll, which signals that effort was put into the asset.
When handed to a designer or developer, this skeleton becomes the section map for the build.
caveats: Placeholder copy is for structure preview only — do not ship placeholder words.
Source gives no conversion data for this format; treat it as a communication and planning tool.

cards.title: Use heatmap software to diagnose where eyes land on a page
cards.summary: A heatmap/prediction tool shows whether attention goes where the page needs it — usually the headline — making page-structure critiques concrete.
cards.use_when: Auditing a landing page, opt-in page, or homepage structure, or showing a stakeholder why the current layout underperforms.
steps: Run the page through a heat tracking or attention-prediction tool. (The source uses one called Expose; verify current tool names and interfaces before relying on any specific product.)
Read the output: deep red is where eyes go first and most. On the example page, attention went to the person's face and the 'Start Now' button — not the headline.

Diagnose the problem: if attention anchors on a vague button, people won't click it because they don't know what's inside. If nothing funnels attention to one primary element, the page has no clear first read.
Fix by making the headline the obvious first stop — specific, outcome-led, and placed where the eye naturally lands.
Re-run the tool on your rewrite and compare the before/after attention pattern to confirm the headline now captures the first look.
Add a clear descriptor to any button (what happens after clicking) so attention on the CTA is not wasted.
caveats: The source presents this as proof, but attention prediction is a heuristic, not a measured conversion result.
Some of these tools model attention rather than record real user clicks or scrolls — verify what you are looking at; pair with session recordings or A/B tests when the stakes are high.

cards.title: Headline formula: time-frame plus discovery plus outcome plus ease
cards.summary: A demonstrated opt-in headline structure bundles a specific time promise, a named method, a concrete outcome, and a no-experience qualifier.
cards.use_when: Writing or rewriting an opt-in page headline, lead-magnet headline, or top-of-funnel ad hook for a store.
steps: Use the source's pattern as a model: 'In the next 10 minutes you're about to discover the copy and paste strategy that people all around the world are using to make over $1,000 a day with affiliate marketing, no experience required — click below to find out how.'

Break it into the four load-bearing parts: (1) time frame ('in the next 10 minutes'), (2) discovery frame ('you're about to discover'), (3) the mechanism ('the copy and paste strategy'), (4) the outcome with specificity ('people all around the world are using to make over $1,000 a day'), plus (5) an ease qualifier ('no experience required'), and (6) a clear next click ('click below to find out how').
For a product or landing page, swap the outcome for the customer's real desired result and the mechanism for your actual method or product feature — never claim a result your offer can't deliver.

Pair the headline with an uncluttered page so the headline is the first thing read; the source's before/after critique centers on a vague headline competing with a photo and a bare 'Start Now' button.
caveats: Specific numeric income claims in the example are the source's illustration, not a benchmark; do not copy income claims you cannot substantiate (ad platforms and regulators police these).
This structure is one option; the source also stresses not copying templates word for word.

cards.title: Deliver a built resource, not a long critique, to earn trust
cards.summary: Critique is cheap; handing over a finished asset (rewritten page, sample emails) is what the source says actually gets replies and demonstrates skill.
cards.use_when: Approaching a store owner or partner about improving their site, emails, or ads — or producing outreach creative for wholesale/retail accounts.
steps: Do not send a long commentary about what is wrong. The source argues a 10–20 minute talking-head critique is not valuable because it isn't a usable asset.
Build the thing instead: recreate their landing page, write three emails on their list, or draft alternative ad copy for their product.
Walk them through it briefly in a short recorded video, or a concise written breakdown, showing what you changed and why.
Lead with the rebuilt asset so the recipient sees the finished output first; the source's example opens the Loom by showing their version of the page.
Keep the scope small enough to deliver fast — the point is a short, made-for-them resource, not a full engagement delivered for free.
caveats: Free spec work has cost and opportunity cost; the source assumes you can produce assets quickly enough to make it worthwhile.
Do not misrepresent the rebuilt asset as live or results-backed — it is a demonstration.

cards.title: Personal brand account = professional personal profile, not an ad feed
cards.summary: A credible personal Instagram profile (varied, high-value personal posts with occasional business content and no hard CTAs) builds trust when prospects check you out.
cards.use_when: Building or cleaning up the founder/operator or brand-adjacent social profile that prospects, wholesale buyers, or partners will inspect before engaging.
steps: Post content from your personal life, but keep it professional — no crude memes, no oversharing about relationships or nights out. The profile should read as 'a real, non-sketchy person,' not 'one big advertisement.'
Do not make every post a hard sell ('DM me if you want to make 10x revenue'). The source says the profile should look personal, and only sometimes mention what you do.
Post regularly. Treat the profile as an ongoing asset, not a one-time setup.
Use proven post formats but add your own content — do not copy templates verbatim.

Three easy formats demonstrated: (1) high-value hobby post (you doing an activity you enjoy, with a casual caption), (2) talking-head video about business or life with a hook, (3) photo with a testimonial underneath and a short caption.
Avoid multiple CTAs ('DM me for email marketing'). The source calls this weak and desperate-looking.
For store operators, this same profile logic applies to the founder account that wholesale buyers and press will look at — a real person behind the brand, not a wall of product links.
caveats: This is the source's subjective taste on what reads as credible; results are anecdotal.
You do not need luxury props — the source explicitly says a cheap item or a good outdoor photo works, and that association alone influences perception.

cards.title: Make business content, not craft content, for owner audiences
cards.summary: The source argues copywriters lose business by posting about copywriting technique; business owners only engage with content about money, results, and their own problems.
cards.use_when: Planning content that should attract store owners or business decision-makers — founder-led content, guest posts, outreach follow-ups, or case-study posts.
steps: Translate craft topics into business outcomes. Instead of 'the top 5 subject lines' or 'the PAS formula,' frame content as 'here's how to make more money with proper email, landing page setup, and funnel optimization.'

Use result-led hooks: 'How I got an extra $20,000/month for my fitness client — I optimized his emails, recreated his CTAs, and fixed his sales pages.' For a store: 'How we lifted repeat purchase rate by fixing the post-purchase email sequence' (only if true).

Use the 'in my experience' frame to convey authority: 'If a niche business struggles booking qualified calls, in my experience it comes down to these two things...' The source notes you can also borrow established marketers' authority by citing what they say.

Convert into a numbered how-to: 'Three easiest ways to grow your email list and milk it for every penny it's worth — 1... 2... 3...' Businesses understand and want this; they don't care about the internal jargon of your discipline.
Test your draft: would a store owner read this and think about their own revenue, or would only another marketer find it interesting? If the latter, rewrite.
caveats: The source asserts a clear rule ('create content for business owners, not copywriters') as its opinion, not a measured finding.
Any result claims in your content must be true and verifiable for your own clients or store — the example figures are the source's illustration.

cards.title: Reach out to owners on the channel where they actually engage
cards.summary: The source's method for identifying business owners is to look for people actively spending on ads and building audiences, since that signals budget and an existing offer.
cards.use_when: Finding potential wholesale accounts, affiliate partners, or brands to collaborate with — or as a model for finding where your own ideal customers gather.
steps: Scroll the platform and click on ads. A business running ads to a post is spending money, which is the signal the source looks for.

Open the advertiser's profile and check the numbers — followers, engagement, whether their bio names a role like 'Founder/CEO' or a revenue claim. The source treats a visible offer and a real business as qualifying factors.
Prefer mid-sized accounts over the largest ones. The source's stated logic: a 10,000-follower business owner is far more likely to actually see and answer a message than one with 500,000+ followers.

Follow the suggested-profiles rail ('followed by' and 'you may also like') from a qualified prospect to find more in the same circle. The source finds 'five or six potential clients in about 30 seconds' this way.

On YouTube, search the topic your buyer would search ('how to run ads') and target mid-sized channels with an offer or opt-in link, skipping the biggest channels and the ones with no link or unrelated content.

If no email is listed, the source suggests moving to another platform (Instagram, LinkedIn) or a contact-finding tool such as Apollo — verify the current tool's data coverage and terms before use, and follow platform rules on unsolicited contact.
caveats: Advertising spend is the source's proxy for budget; it does not prove the business is a good fit or responsive.
Following accounts causes the platform to show you more of their ads — useful for prospecting, but be aware of algorithmic bias in the sample you collect.

cards.title: Opener writes itself when you reply to something specific they posted
cards.summary: A low-friction conversation starter: reply to or reference a specific recent post, name what you liked, and end with one short question.
cards.use_when: Sending the first message to a prospective partner, wholesale buyer, affiliate, or account — or adapting this as the first message in a cold email sequence.
steps: Find a specific recent post, story, or video from the person — not their profile in general. The source scrolls back to older posts if nothing is recent.
Open by naming the specific thing you liked: 'I really liked how you did X.' This is a genuine reference, not flattery, and it proves you consumed their content.
Close with one simple, short question — not a pitch, not a request for a call.
If you are replying to a story or post, keep the reply short and relatable rather than immediately pitching your service.
Avoid the generic opener; the source's rationale is that a specific reference signals you are a real person engaging with their work.
caveats: This is the source's outreach method for starting business conversations; it is not a substitute for the built-asset follow-up that actually earns the reply.
Platform rules and spam filters shape deliverability — keep first messages short, specific, and non-promotional to avoid the promotions tab or spam folder.

cards.title: Quality is more important than quantity — but only quantity teaches quality
cards.summary: Two rules the source calls universal: ship the highest-quality asset you can, and accept that the way to learn quality is to produce a high volume of work.
cards.use_when: Planning any content or copy practice schedule — product descriptions, emails, ad variations — and deciding whether to publish or keep iterating.
steps: Rule 1: make each asset you ship as high quality as you can — polish the specific piece in front of you. Do not let volume become an excuse for sloppy output.

Rule 2: accept that your first hundred pieces are practice. 'Your 101st email will be higher quality than the best email you could ever make as your first email.' Volume is how you learn the craft, not a contradiction of quality.

Practical application for a store: batch-produce variations (say, 100 product descriptions or email subject lines), publish the strongest, and keep the rest as a refinement pool. Each cycle improves your judgment about what works.
Do not let the pursuit of quality stall production entirely — the source's claim is that quality emerges from reps, so both rules apply at once.
Review what you produced after a batch and identify patterns in what held up, rather than judging each piece in isolation.
caveats: The '100 pieces' idea is the source's rhetorical illustration, not a measured threshold.
High volume without review does not automatically produce quality — the source assumes you are comparing and improving across reps.

cards.title: When something 'doesn't work,' audit execution before abandoning the channel
cards.summary: The source's recurring theme: if a tactic failed for you, look at how well you executed it, because most people who call a channel dead are doing it badly.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to abandon or double down on an underperforming channel — email, video, ads, a landing page format — before writing it off.
steps: Audit output quality against the standard the tactic requires. The source's example is video: people say video doesn't work, then look at their video and it runs two minutes without actually saying anything useful.
Check the length and density of the asset first — the source's test is whether the asset delivers value quickly and densely, not whether the channel is oversaturated.
Look at whether the required building block is even present: a clear headline, a reason to act, a specific audience, a real result shown.
Only after confirming execution quality is adequate consider the possibility that the channel or tactic is genuinely wrong for the audience.

Track the distinction between lead conversion (a form filled, a reply) and purchase conversion (an order placed) when diagnosing failures — a channel can generate the first and fail at the second for unrelated reasons.
Give a channel enough reps before judging it, consistent with the source's argument that skill, not saturation, is usually the constraint.
caveats: This can become an excuse to keep pouring money into a channel that isn't returning — pair it with real cost and conversion data.
The source presents this as an opinion ('if you do it super well... big things happen'); it is not a measured finding across channels.
